newsitem.title: HONG KONG: UK did too much,too late in HK -- Singapore's Lee.
newsitem.headline: UK did too much,too late in HK -- Singapore's Lee.

text.p: Singapore's founding father Lee Kuan Yew accused Britain on Tuesday of doing too much, too late by bringing democracy to Hong Kong in the final years before the colony's handover to China.

Launching a forthright attack on London in the last week before the transfer of power, Lee said colonial Governor Chris Patten's political reforms had given the United States a stick to beat China with.
But Lee was confident that Washington and Beijing could work out any differences. If they didn't, then Hong Kong would fail, he warned.

Lee, who led Singapore to independence from Britain in the early 1960s, told a Hong Kong business conference: "The British have tried to implement a political agenda for Hong Kong. It was too much, too late.
"Patten's political agenda has provided a stick for foreign lobby groups to beat China with. The U.S. media, human rights groups and Congress have taken up this stick."

Patten was vilified by Beijing and called a criminal and prostitute for bringing limited democratic reforms to Hong Kong in the run-up to the June 30 handover of the colony after 156 years of colonial rule.

Singapore's elder statesman said China would go out of its way to ensure that Hong Kong would prosper economically but said of the communist giant: "It will not tolerate politicking in Hong Kong that will disturb China's political system."
Lee, whose city state is like Hong Kong a bustling free market economy, locked horns at the conference with Hugh Davies, Britain's chief negotiator with China over the handover.
Davies took issue with Lee over his criticism, saying: "Hong Kong is in better shape than it has ever been .. I think we have come out pretty well."
But Lee, Singapore's prime minister until 1990 and now government senior minister, said London's efforts had been belated and misconceived.
"I think the British side did not live up to its highest tradition," he told the "countdown conference" organised by the Far Eastern Economic Review.
"At the tail end of empire, the British thought primarily of themselves and not the people of Hong Kong," he said.
